EXAMPLE REGIONAL MEDICAL CENTER - ED PROVIDER NOTE
TESTPATIENT, CASEY   MRN 7741902   DOB 01/01/1964   11/08/2024   Provider: Dr. H. Example, MD

HPI: 60 yo F on apixaban for AF presents after mechanical fall at a grocery store ~30 min prior to arrival. Slipped on liquid, fell backward, struck back of head on tile floor and landed on R elbow. No LOC per pt and bystander. Has diffuse HA 6/10, nausea, vomited once. Denies vision change, weakness, numbness, neck pain, CP, palpitations beyond baseline. No preceding dizziness or syncope prior to slipping. R elbow pain with movement.

Exam: BP 158/90, HR 84 irregularly irregular. Alert, oriented x3, GCS 15, speech fluent.
Head: 2 cm linear laceration occipital scalp, hemostatic with pressure, small surrounding hematoma. No step-off.
Neck: no midline tenderness, full painless ROM (Canadian C-spine rule: low risk, able to rotate 45 deg).
Neuro: CN intact, no pronator drift, finger-nose normal, gait deferred initially.
R elbow: tenderness over olecranon and radial head, mild swelling, ROM 20-120 deg limited by pain, no effusion palpable. NV intact distally.

MDM: Head trauma on DOAC = high risk for ICH. CT head and C-spine not indicated by rule but CT head obtained stat. XR R elbow.
11:12 CT head: no acute intracranial hemorrhage, no fracture; small occipital subgaleal hematoma.
11:30 XR R elbow: no fracture, no joint effusion.
11:40 Laceration repaired: irrigated with 250 mL NS, 4 staples placed. Tolerated well.
12:15 Ondansetron given, nausea resolved, tolerating PO. Ambulated with steady gait.

Discussed with pt: given negative CT and normal neuro exam, observation at home with responsible adult is reasonable; risk of delayed bleed on anticoagulation discussed. Pt's husband will stay with her. Continue apixaban per discussion (low risk of delayed ICH vs stroke risk from AF; CHA2DS2-VASc 2).

EXAMPLE REGIONAL MEDICAL CENTER - EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT
Discharge Instructions

Name: TESTPATIENT, JORDAN     DOB: 01/01/1979     Visit date: 06/02/2024
Your diagnosis today: CLOSED NONDISPLACED FRACTURE OF THE RIGHT DISTAL RADIUS

ABOUT WRIST FRACTURES
A fracture is a break in a bone. The radius is one of the two bones of the forearm. A break near the wrist is one of the most common fractures in adults, often from falling on an outstretched hand. A nondisplaced fracture means the pieces of bone have stayed in line.

CARING FOR YOUR SPLINT
- Keep your splint clean and dry. Cover it with a plastic bag when bathing.
- Do not put anything inside the splint to scratch.
- Keep your arm raised above the level of your heart as much as possible for the next 2-3 days to reduce swelling.
- Apply ice over the splint (not directly on skin) for 20 minutes at a time.
- Move your fingers often.

PAIN
You may take the pain medicine prescribed today as directed. Do not drive while taking medicine that makes you drowsy.

FOLLOW UP
See the orthopedic clinic (Example Orthopedics, 555-0133) in 5 to 7 days. You will likely need a repeat X-ray and a cast.

RETURN TO THE EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT IF:
- Your fingers become numb, cold, pale, or blue
- Pain is much worse and not helped by medicine
- The splint feels too tight or gets wet or broken

OPERATIVE REPORT

PATIENT: TESTPATIENT, JORDAN        DOB: 01/01/1984       MRN: ESC-30217
DATE OF SURGERY: 04/02/2024
SURGEON: E. Example, MD             ASSISTANT: T. Example, PA-C
ANESTHESIA: General (LMA) with right adductor canal block

PREOPERATIVE DIAGNOSIS: Right knee medial meniscus tear with displaced fragment.
POSTOPERATIVE DIAGNOSIS: Right knee complex tear posterior horn medial meniscus
with displaced flap; grade II chondromalacia medial femoral condyle.

PROCEDURES PERFORMED:
1. Right knee arthroscopy with partial medial meniscectomy (29881).
2. Removal of displaced meniscal fragment from posteromedial recess.
3. Diagnostic arthroscopy of patellofemoral and lateral compartments.

INDICATIONS: 40-year-old male with right knee pain, catching and giving way
after a twisting work injury on 02/12/2024. MRI 03/01/2024 demonstrated a
posterior horn medial meniscus tear with displaced flap fragment. Symptoms
persisted despite activity modification, bracing and NSAIDs. Risks, benefits and
alternatives were discussed and he elected to proceed.

DESCRIPTION OF PROCEDURE: The patient was identified in the preoperative area
and the right knee was marked. He was brought to the operating room and general
anesthesia was induced. A well-padded thigh holder was applied, and the
contralateral leg was positioned in a well-leg holder. Examination under
anesthesia showed full range of motion with stable Lachman, drawer, and varus/
valgus testing. The leg was prepped and draped in standard sterile fashion. A
time-out was performed. Cefazolin was given prior to incision.

Standard anterolateral and anteromedial portals were established. Diagnostic
arthroscopy was performed. The suprapatellar pouch showed mild synovitis and no
loose bodies. The patellofemoral joint showed normal articular cartilage and
normal tracking. The medial gutter was clear. In the medial compartment there
was a complex horizontal-oblique tear of the posterior horn of the medial
meniscus with an inferior leaf flap that was unstable to probing. The tear
extended into the white-white and red-white zones and was not amenable to
repair. A displaced fragment approximately 6 mm was identified in the

label: procedure_report
note: continuation starting mid-sentence
text:
posteromedial recess, visualized through the notch with the 70-degree scope,
and was retrieved with a grasper and sent to pathology. Using basket punches and
a 4.0 mm shaver, partial medial meniscectomy was performed of the unstable flap
and torn inferior leaf back to a stable, contoured rim, removing approximately
25% of the posterior horn. The remaining meniscus was stable to probing. The
medial femoral condyle showed an area of grade II softening and fibrillation,
approximately 1 x 1 cm, which was stable and not debrided. The medial tibial
plateau was intact.

The intercondylar notch showed intact ACL and PCL. The lateral compartment
showed an intact lateral meniscus and normal articular cartilage.

The knee was copiously irrigated and all instruments removed. Portals were
closed with 3-0 nylon. 20 mL of 0.25% bupivacaine was injected into the joint.
Sterile dressing and a cold therapy wrap were applied.

SPECIMENS: Medial meniscus fragment to pathology.
ESTIMATED BLOOD LOSS: Minimal.
COMPLICATIONS: None.
DRAINS: None.
IMPLANTS: None.  TOURNIQUET: Applied, not inflated.
CONDITION: Stable to PACU.

POSTOPERATIVE PLAN: Weight-bearing as tolerated with crutches for 3-5 days.
Begin PT for knee within 1 week. Aspirin 81 mg BID x 2 weeks for DVT
prophylaxis. Oxycodone/acetaminophen 5/325 #12 for breakthrough pain; ice and
elevation. Follow up 10-14 days for suture removal.

PROCEDURE REPORT

PATIENT: TESTPATIENT, JORDAN   DOB: 01/01/1984   DATE: 03/21/2024
PHYSICIAN: L. Example, MD

PROCEDURE: Left L5-S1 transforaminal epidural steroid injection under
fluoroscopic guidance with contrast epidurography.

PRE-OPERATIVE DIAGNOSIS: Left S1 radiculopathy; L5-S1 disc extrusion.
POST-OPERATIVE DIAGNOSIS: Same.
ANESTHESIA: Local only.
INDICATIONS: Persistent left S1 radicular pain >4 weeks despite NSAIDs, oral
steroid and physical therapy, with concordant MRI findings.

DESCRIPTION OF PROCEDURE:
After informed consent was obtained, the patient was placed prone on the
fluoroscopy table. A time-out was performed confirming patient, procedure and
left side. The lumbosacral region was prepped with chlorhexidine and draped in
sterile fashion. Under AP and oblique fluoroscopy the left S1 superior foramen
was identified. The skin was anesthetized with 3 mL of 1% lidocaine. A 22-gauge
3.5-inch spinal needle was advanced under intermittent fluoroscopy to the
superior lateral aspect of the left S1 foramen. Lateral view confirmed depth.
After negative aspiration for blood and CSF, 1.5 mL of Omnipaque 240 was
injected under live fluoroscopy demonstrating outlining of the left S1 nerve
root and epidural spread without vascular uptake. Then 10 mg of preservative-
free dexamethasone with 1 mL of normal saline was injected slowly. The needle
was removed and a bandage applied.

The patient tolerated the procedure well with no complications. Estimated blood
loss: none. Pre-procedure pain 6/10; post-procedure 2/10 (leg).

DISPOSITION: Discharged in stable condition to spouse. Written instructions
provided. Follow up 2 weeks. Pain diary given.

text:
EXAMPLE SURGERY CENTER
KNEE ARTHROSCOPY: GOING HOME

What is knee arthroscopy?
Knee arthroscopy is a procedure in which a surgeon looks inside the knee joint
using a small camera through two or three small cuts. Common reasons include
torn meniscus cartilage, loose pieces of cartilage, and irritation of the joint
lining.

Pain and swelling
- Most people have moderate soreness for the first 3-5 days.
- Keep your leg raised above the level of your heart when resting.
- Use ice or the cold wrap for 20 minutes at a time, several times a day.
  Always keep a cloth between the ice and your skin.
- Take pain medicine as directed by your surgeon.

Dressing and incisions
- Keep the dressing clean and dry for 48 hours.
- After 48 hours you may remove the bulky dressing and cover each small cut
  with a bandage strip.
- You may shower after 48 hours. Do not soak in a bath, pool or hot tub until
  your stitches are out and the cuts are healed.
- Some pink fluid draining through the dressing on the first day is normal.

Activity
- Use crutches as instructed. Most patients may put weight on the leg as
  comfortable unless told otherwise.
- Do ankle pumps (move your foot up and down) 10 times every hour while awake.
- Do not drive while using crutches or taking opioid pain medicine.

label: education_handout
note: continuation page of generic handout
text:
- Return to desk work is often possible in a few days; physical jobs may take
  4-6 weeks depending on the procedure done.

Exercises to start the day after surgery
  Quad sets: tighten the muscle on the front of your thigh, pushing the back of
  the knee down. Hold 5 seconds. Repeat 10 times, 3 times a day.
  Straight leg raises: tighten the thigh, then lift the straight leg 12 inches.
  Hold 3 seconds. Repeat 10 times.
  Heel slides: slide your heel toward your buttock, bending the knee as far as
  comfortable. Repeat 10 times.

Call your surgeon if you have:
- Temperature over 101.5 F
- Redness, warmth, or pus-like drainage from the incisions
- Increasing pain not helped by medicine
- Calf pain or swelling, especially if one calf is larger than the other
- Numbness or tingling in the foot that does not go away

Call 911 for chest pain or sudden shortness of breath.

label: education_handout
text:
BLOOD CLOTS AFTER SURGERY (DVT)

A deep vein thrombosis (DVT) is a blood clot in a deep vein, usually in the leg.
Clots are more likely after surgery, after long trips, and when you move less.
A piece of a clot can travel to the lungs, which is an emergency.

Ways to lower your risk:
- Walk short distances several times a day as allowed.
- Do ankle pumps while sitting or lying down.
- Drink plenty of fluids.
- Take any blood-thinning medicine exactly as prescribed.

Signs of a clot in the leg: swelling, pain or calf cramping. Signs of a clot in the lung: sudden shortness of breath,
chest pain, coughing up blood - call 911.

text:
** TESTPATIENT, JORDAN   DOB 01/01/1984   EXAMPLE REHAB CENTER **

LOW BACK EXERCISES: EXTENSION PROGRAM

These exercises are often used for back pain that feels better when you stand
or walk and worse when you sit or bend forward. Stop any exercise that makes
pain spread further down your leg.

1. Lying on your stomach
   Lie face down with arms at your sides and head turned to one side.
   Relax completely for 2-3 minutes.

2. Prone on elbows
   From lying face down, prop yourself up on your elbows. Let your hips and
   low back sag. Breathe deeply. Hold 2-3 minutes.

3. Press-ups
   Lie face down with hands under your shoulders, as for a push-up. Keep your
   hips on the floor and slowly straighten your elbows to lift your upper body.
   Let your back sag. Hold 1-2 seconds and lower. Repeat 10 times.

4. Standing back bends
   Stand with feet apart and hands on the small of your back. Lean backward
   as far as comfortable, keeping knees straight. Repeat 10 times.

How often: every 2-3 hours during the day, or as your therapist directs.

Good signs: pain moves toward the center of your back, even if back pain
increases a little.
Warning signs: pain moves further into the buttock or leg, or new numbness.

If your pain spreads into your leg while doing these, try the same movement
with your hips shifted slightly away from the painful side, and talk with your
therapist before continuing.

Sitting tips: use a small rolled towel in the curve of your low back. Stand up
and do a back bend every 30 minutes.

distances. He denies prior knee injury or surgery. Pain today 5/10 at rest, 8/10
with stairs. He continues on ibuprofen. He is also being treated by his PCP for

EXAMPLE PATHOLOGY ASSOCIATES
Surgical Pathology Report                 Accession: SP24-004412

Patient: TESTPATIENT, JORDAN    DOB: 01/01/1984    Sex: M
Submitting: E. Example, MD, Example Surgery Center
Procedure date: 04/02/2024    Received: 04/02/2024    Reported: 04/05/2024

CLINICAL HISTORY: Right knee twisting injury 02/2024; medial meniscus tear with
displaced flap.

SPECIMEN: Right knee, medial meniscus fragment and debris.

GROSS DESCRIPTION:
Received in formalin labeled with the patient's name and "R knee medial
meniscus" are multiple fragments of rubbery, white-tan fibrocartilaginous tissue
measuring 1.4 x 0.9 x 0.3 cm in aggregate, the largest a crescentic fragment
measuring 0.6 x 0.4 x 0.3 cm. Entirely submitted in one cassette (A1).

MICROSCOPIC DESCRIPTION:
Sections show fragments of fibrocartilage with frayed and fissured edges.
There is focal myxoid (mucoid) degeneration and mild chondrocyte clustering,
features that are often seen in meniscal tissue of adults and may coexist with
acute tears. Along one edge there is a thin layer of fibrin with entrapped red
blood cells and scant reactive fibroblastic proliferation, compatible with a
recent (weeks) tear surface. No crystal deposition is identified under
polarized light. No inflammatory arthropathy, no synovial proliferation of
concern, and no neoplasm is present.

DIAGNOSIS:
Right knee, medial meniscus, arthroscopic excision:
  - Fragmented fibrocartilage (meniscus) with tear-related changes, including
    surface fibrin consistent with recent injury, and mild myxoid degeneration.
  - Negative for crystals, inflammatory arthritis, and malignancy.

Dear Ms. Example:

As you know, this firm represents Jordan Testpatient for injuries suffered
in the collision of March 2, 2024. This letter sets out the facts, our
client's injuries and treatment, and our demand for settlement within your
insured's policy limits.

I. LIABILITY

On March 2, 2024, at approximately 5:40 p.m., our client was stopped at a red
light at Example Avenue and Sample Street when your insured, traveling an
estimated 35 mph, struck the rear of our client's vehicle without braking.
The investigating officer cited your insured for following too closely and
inattentive driving. Your insured admitted at the scene that he was looking
at his phone. Liability is clear and we do not expect it to be disputed.

II. INJURIES AND TREATMENT

Mr. Testpatient was restrained and the airbags did not deploy. His head
struck the headrest and he felt immediate pain in his neck. Example County
Fire/EMS evaluated him at the scene; he was placed in a cervical collar and
transported to Example Community Hospital. In the emergency department he
reported neck pain of 8/10, low back pain, and right-sided chest pain from
the seat belt. CT of the head and cervical spine showed no fracture. He was
diagnosed with cervical and lumbar sprain and a right chest wall contusion,
given ketorolac and morphine, and discharged with a soft collar,
cyclobenzaprine and instructions to follow up with his primary physician.

Three days later he saw his primary care physician, reporting worsening neck
pain and new tingling into the right thumb and index finger, and headaches
at the base of the skull most afternoons. He was referred to physical
therapy and for MRI. MRI of the cervical spine on April 9, 2024 showed a
C5-6 disc protrusion contacting the right C6 nerve root, with no prior
imaging for comparison.

He began physical therapy at Example Physical Therapy & Rehab on April 24,
2024 and attended 21 visits through August 5, 2024. At intake his Neck
Disability Index was 48% (severe); at discharge it had improved to 26%.

Because radicular symptoms persisted, he was referred to Dr. D. Example at
Example Spine Clinic, who diagnosed C6 radiculopathy and performed a
cervical interlaminar epidural steroid injection on May 16, 2024, which gave
roughly 50% relief for six weeks. Right C5-6 and C6-7 medial branch blocks
followed on June 27, 2024 for persistent axial neck pain. Dr. Example has
documented that our client may require radiofrequency ablation and, if the
radicular pain recurs, a surgical consultation.

Our client is a delivery driver. He missed eleven days of work and then
worked restricted duty (no lifting over 25 lb) for nine weeks, during which
he was unable to work his usual overtime.

III. IMPACT ON DAILY LIFE

Before the collision, Mr. Testpatient played in a weekend soccer league and
coached his daughter's team. He has not returned to either. He reports he
cannot turn his head fully to check his blind spot, wakes two to three times
a night from neck pain, and feels anxious driving through intersections.
His spouse has taken over yard work and carrying groceries.

RE: SETTLEMENT DEMAND - TIME LIMITED

Dear Mr. Example:

As you know, this firm represents Alex Testpatient for injuries he sustained on June 3,
2024, when your insured ran a red light at Example Ave and 4th St and struck the
passenger side of our client's vehicle. The responding officer cited your insured for
failure to obey a traffic signal, and an independent witness confirmed that your
insured entered the intersection on red. Liability is not reasonably in dispute.

INJURIES AND TREATMENT

Mr. Testpatient was transported by Example County Fire Rescue to the Example Community
Hospital emergency department complaining of neck and low back pain. Radiographs showed
no fracture, and he was discharged with diagnoses of cervical and lumbar strain.

He followed up with his family physician, Dr. D. Example, on June 11, 2024, reporting
low back pain radiating into his left leg, and was referred to physical therapy. Despite
therapy, on July 2 he developed tingling in his left foot and pain extending to the
ankle. An MRI on July 8, 2024 revealed a left paracentral disc extrusion at L4-L5
displacing the left L5 nerve root, with an annular fissure and paraspinal edema
consistent with acute injury.

On August 6, 2024 he underwent a left L4-L5 and L5-S1 transforaminal epidural steroid
injection at Example Spine & Pain Center, which provided temporary relief. Dr. J.
Example has documented that if symptoms recur he may be a candidate for a left L4-L5
microdiscectomy, estimated at $38,000 to $45,000.

What is whip1ash?
Whip1ash is an injury to the muscles, ligaments and other soft tissues of the neck
caused by a sudden back-and-forth movement of the head, such as in a rear-end car

text:
07/01/2024 08:31 FROM 555-0233 EXAMPLE ORTHOPEDICS          FAX P.004/009

EXAMPLE SURGERY CENTER
OPERATIVE REPORT

Patient: TESTPATIENT, RILEY          DOB: 01/01/1988          MRN: ESC-11873
Date of surgery: 06/24/2024          Surgeon: C. Example, MD
Assistant: DD. Example, PA-C         Anesthesia: EE. Example, MD (general LMA + adductor canal block)

PREOPERATIVE DIAGNOSIS: Left knee medial meniscus tear (S83.242A), work injury 04/09/2024.
POSTOPERATIVE DIAGNOSES:
 1. Left knee complex tear, posterior horn and body of the medial meniscus.
 2. Grade II chondromalacia, medial femoral condyle.
 3. Mild synovitis, suprapatellar pouch.

PROCEDURES:
 1. Left knee arthroscopy with partial medial meniscectomy (CPT 29881).
 2. Limited synovectomy, suprapatellar pouch.
 3. Chondroplasty, medial femoral condyle (included).

INDICATIONS: 36-year-old male roofer's helper who fell approximately 6 feet from a ladder
at work on 04/09/2024, landing on the left knee. He has had persistent medial knee pain,
recurrent effusions, catching and two episodes of locking despite bracing, activity
modification, NSAIDs and a period of physical therapy. MRI on 05/24/2024 demonstrated a
complex tear of the posterior horn of the medial meniscus with a bone bruise of the
medial tibial plateau. Risks, benefits and alternatives, including infection, bleeding,
DVT/PE, stiffness, persistent pain, nerve or vessel injury, need for further surgery and
the possibility of meniscal repair versus resection, were discussed at length, and the
patient elected to proceed. Consent was signed and the left knee was marked in preop.

DESCRIPTION OF PROCEDURE: The patient was identified in the preoperative holding area
and an adductor canal block was placed by anesthesia. He was brought to the operating
room and placed supine. After induction of general anesthesia via LMA, cefazolin 2 g IV
was given within 60 minutes of incision. A well-padded thigh tourniquet was placed but
not inflated. The left leg was placed in a leg holder and the contralateral leg in a
well-leg holder with padding of all bony prominences. The left lower extremity was
prepped and draped in the usual sterile fashion. A time-out confirmed correct patient,
side and procedure.

Standard anterolateral and anteromedial portals were created. Diagnostic arthroscopy
was performed. The suprapatellar pouch showed mild hypertrophic synovitis, which was
debrided with a shaver. The patellofemoral joint showed normal articular cartilage with
good tracking. The lateral gutter and medial gutter were free of loose bodies.

label: procedure_report
note: Headerless continuation of the operative report: medial compartment findings, closure, plan.
text:
In the medial compartment, with valgus stress applied, there was a complex tear involving
the posterior horn and extending into the body of the medial meniscus, with a horizontal
cleavage component and an unstable radial flap displaceable into the notch on probing.
The tear was in the white-white zone and not amenable to repair. Using a combination of
straight and up-biting basket punches and a 4.0 mm shaver, the unstable portion was
resected back to a stable, smoothly contoured rim, removing approximately 30% of the
meniscal width in the posterior horn and 15% in the body. The remaining meniscus was
probed and found stable. The medial femoral condyle showed an area of grade II
fibrillation approximately 1.5 x 1 cm in the weight-bearing zone, which was lightly
debrided with the shaver to a stable border. The medial tibial plateau cartilage was
intact.

The intercondylar notch demonstrated an intact anterior cruciate ligament with good
tension on probing and an intact posterior cruciate ligament. The lateral compartment
showed an intact lateral meniscus on probing and normal articular cartilage.

The knee was copiously irrigated and all instruments were removed. Portals were closed
with 3-0 nylon simple interrupted sutures. 20 mL of 0.25% bupivacaine was injected into
the joint and portal sites. A sterile dressing, cryotherapy cuff and compression wrap
were applied. The tourniquet was never inflated. The patient was awakened and taken to
PACU in stable condition.

FINDINGS: As above. Photographs taken and placed in chart.
ESTIMATED BLOOD LOSS: minimal.   FLUIDS: 800 mL LR.   DRAINS: none.
SPECIMENS: none.   COMPLICATIONS: none apparent.   COUNTS: correct x2.

POSTOPERATIVE PLAN:
 - Weight bearing as tolerated with crutches for comfort, wean over 3-5 days.
 - Aspirin 81 mg BID x 2 weeks for DVT prophylaxis.
 - Oxycodone-acetaminophen 5/325 mg 1 tab q6h PRN, #20; ondansetron 4 mg PRN nausea.
 - Begin PT within 1 week: ROM, quad activation, gait training.
 - Work: off work 2 weeks, then seated duty; anticipate return to ladder and roof work
   in 6-8 weeks depending on progress. Workers' comp work status form provided.
 - Follow up in clinic 10-14 days for suture removal.

Prognosis discussed: given chondral changes and the amount of meniscus resected, he has
an increased long-term risk of medial compartment arthritis.

C. Example, MD - Orthopedic Surgery        Dictated 06/24/2024 12:10  Signed 06/25/2024

the left L4-L5 foramen was identified. Skin and subcutaneous tissue anesthetized with

Lateral view confirmed position. Negative aspiration for blood/CSF. Omnipaque 240,
1 mL, showed epidural spread along the L5 nerve root and into the epidural space
without vascular uptake on live fluoroscopy. Injected dexamethasone 10 mg (preservative
free) with 1 mL 1% lidocaine (PF). Same procedure at left L5-S1 with dexamethasone
5 mg. Needles removed intact, bandages applied.

EBL: minimal. Complications: none. Patient tolerated well.
Pre-procedure pain 7/10, post-procedure 2/10. Strength 5/5 bilateral LE post-procedure.
